name: Maximal independent set by agents
summary: $n$ agents in an anonymous graph must mark a maximal independent set of nodes.
statement: $n$ agents with distinct identifiers (IDs) are placed on the nodes of an anonymous port-labelled graph with $n$ nodes, $m$ edges and maximum degree $\Delta$. The start is rooted (all agents on one node), dispersed (one agent on each node) or arbitrary. Agents compute only by moving and by talking with agents on the same node. The agents must settle on the nodes of a maximal independent set, every other agent knowing it is not in the set: every agent (or node) learns its part of the output. **Time** is in synchronous rounds; **memory** in bits per agent.

primer.intro: Imagine a building with $n$ rooms that carry no names, and $n$ **agents** (small mobile computers) who must choose some rooms to stand in so that no two chosen rooms are next to each other, yet every room is either chosen or next to a chosen room. The building is a **graph**: rooms are its **nodes** and corridors are its **edges**; there are $n$ nodes and $m$ edges, and from here on we say only node and edge. Two nodes joined by an edge are *neighbours*. The **degree** $\deg(v)$ of a node $v$ is the number of edges at it, and $\Delta$ is the maximum degree. Nodes have no names, but the edges at a node are numbered $1, 2, \dots$; these numbers are **ports**. Each agent has a distinct **identifier** (ID). A set of nodes in which no two nodes are neighbours is *independent*; it is a **maximal independent set** (MIS) if no further node can be added to it without losing this. The agents move in synchronous **rounds** (in each round every agent may talk to the agents on its node, then move along at most one edge), and at the end every agent must know whether it stands on a chosen node. We count rounds and bits of memory per agent. As for all problems in this family, a general method is to make the agents **dispersed** (one agent on each node) and then let them imitate a classical message-passing algorithm by visiting their neighbours (explained under leader election by agents).

ideas.title: Depth-first walk that colours as it settles
ideas.idea:
All $n$ agents start together on one node (a *rooted* start) and know nothing about the graph.

1. The group moves through the graph in a **depth-first walk**: it leaves its current node by a port not tried yet when there is one, and otherwise goes back to the node from which it reached the current node. Whenever it reaches an empty node, the agent with the smallest ID among those still walking stays there for good: it becomes a **settled agent**, and it remembers the port by which the group came in, so the group can later walk back.
2. Before the group moves on, the new settled agent checks its neighbours. If its **parent** (the node from which the walk reached it) holds a *black* agent, it colours itself *grey*. Otherwise it visits every neighbour and comes back: if some neighbour is black it becomes grey, else black.
3. The rest of the group continues the depth-first walk; finding a settled agent on a node tells it that the node was visited before, so it turns back.
4. When every agent has settled, the black agents form the answer.
ideas.analysis: A black agent never has a black neighbour, so the black nodes are independent; every grey agent has a black neighbour, so no node can be added: the set is maximal. The depth-first walk crosses each edge a constant number of times, and the neighbour checks cost $2\deg(v)$ rounds at each node $v$, which sums to $4m$; so the total is $O(m)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits per agent [Chand2023Cover]. The current best without knowledge, from any start, is $O(\max\{n\log^2 n, m\})$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits [Kaur2026MIS].
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that settling agents one at a time along a depth-first walk gives a greedy algorithm for free, the same pattern as dispersion.

ideas.title: Some agent must walk almost the whole diameter
ideas.idea: Let all agents start on the end $s$ of a path with $D+1$ nodes, so the *diameter* $D$ (largest distance between two nodes) is the length of the path. Maximality says that the far end $u$ or its only neighbour must be chosen, and a chosen node needs an agent standing on it. Both nodes are at distance at least $D-1$ from $s$.
ideas.analysis: An agent moves along at most one edge per round, so no agent reaches distance $D-1$ before round $D-1$: from a rooted start every algorithm needs at least $D-1$ rounds. This simple argument is our own, not from the papers; no better lower bound is recorded in the catalogue, so the gap to the known $O(\max\{n\log^2 n, m\})$ rounds is wide open.
ideas.why_it_matters: Distance is the most basic obstacle for moving agents, and the gap between this bound and the known algorithms shows how little is known about the optimal time.

ideas.title: Greedy by identifiers, simulated after dispersion
ideas.idea:
Here the agents know $n$ and $\Delta$, which lets them use the disperse-and-simulate method.

1. Disperse, so that every node holds one agent.
2. Repeat simulated message-passing rounds, each made of $O(\log n)$ blocks of $2\Delta$ rounds in which neighbouring agents meet by the **ID-bit schedule**: in block $i$ an agent whose $i$-th ID bit is $1$ visits its neighbours one by one and an agent whose bit is $0$ waits on its node (see leader election by agents).
3. An agent joins the set as soon as every neighbour with a larger ID has decided and none of them joined; it stays out as soon as some neighbour with a larger ID joined.
4. Each agent tells its neighbours its decision at the next meetings.
ideas.analysis: The agent with the largest ID decides at once, and an agent waits only for neighbours with larger IDs, so a chain of waiting agents has decreasing IDs and at most $n$ members: at most $n$ simulated rounds. Each costs $O(\Delta\log n)$ real rounds, so the total is $O(n\Delta\log n)$ plus the time to disperse, the introductory $O(n\Delta\log n)$ bound of [Pattanayak2024MIS], whose dispersed-start algorithm is this greedy rule with the ID-bit schedule (Theorem 3.4). With $n$ and $\Delta$ known the current best is $O(n\log^2 n + D\Delta\log n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits [Kshemkalyani2026Leader].
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows the cost of the generic method: a slow message-passing algorithm becomes a slow agent algorithm, which is why later work designs algorithms for agents directly.

glossary.definition: the connected, undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on which the agents move, with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges; it is anonymous: its nodes carry no names that an agent can read
an element of $V$; nodes are anonymous
an element of $E$, joining two nodes (which are then neighbours); an agent crosses one edge in one round
the local number $1, \dots, \deg(v)$ that a node $v$ gives to each edge incident to it; the two ends of an edge may carry different numbers
$\deg(v)$, the number of edges at node $v$; $\Delta$ is the maximum degree
a mobile computing entity that moves along edges, talks only with the agents on its own node, and keeps its memory between rounds
the distinct positive integer, at most $L$, that each agent carries; written ID
a synchronous step in which every agent first talks with the agents on its node and then moves along at most one edge
with exactly one agent on every node; a dispersed start begins so, and to disperse is to reach this configuration
a walk of the group of unsettled agents that leaves its current node by a port not tried yet when there is one, and otherwise goes back to the node from which it reached the current node
an agent that the depth-first walk has left on a node for good; a node with a settled agent is occupied, which tells the walking agents it was visited before
for a node $v$ reached by the depth-first walk, the node from which the walk first reached $v$; the settled agent on $v$ remembers the port leading back to it

the meeting schedule in which every agent writes its ID with the same number of bits and time is cut into blocks of $2\Delta$ rounds; in block $i$ the agents whose $i$-th bit is $1$ visit their neighbours one by one (out along one edge, back along it) and the agents whose $i$-th bit is $0$ wait on their nodes, so any two neighbouring agents meet
a set $I \subseteq V$ such that no two nodes of $I$ are joined by an edge and every node outside $I$ has a neighbour in $I$; written MIS

history: MIS by agents was posed with **time first, memory second**: rooted, dispersed and arbitrary starts, trees and grids [Pattanayak2024MIS]; only the rooted algorithm needed no knowledge, and later work removed the knowledge of $n$ and $\Delta$ for every start [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE] [Kaur2026MIS].

axes.name: Knowledge

values.label: $n$ and $\Delta$ are known
values.definition: Every agent knows $n$ and $\Delta$ (upper bounds suffice where stated).

axes.origin: Whether agents know global parameters is inherited from message passing, where nodes typically know $n$ or an upper bound on it, and possibly $\Delta$ and $D$; Kshemkalyani, Kumar, Molla and Sharma set the agent-based model against this and asked for algorithms that rely on no such knowledge, "neither exact nor an upper bound" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Knowing $n$ and $\Delta$ tells an agent how long to wait: in the arbitrary-start minimal dominating set algorithm of Chand, Molla and Sivasubramaniam every robot waits $\kappa n\Delta$ rounds before leader election begins [Chand2023Cover], and the introductory maximal independent set algorithms assume both $n$ and $\Delta$ when the agents start dispersed or arbitrarily placed, but need no knowledge from a rooted start [Pattanayak2024MIS]. Kshemkalyani et al. state the trade-off: solutions without knowledge "are more resilient to network changes and device faults", but "algorithm design becomes challenging since devices may not know how long to run a procedure to guarantee a solution" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Later papers remove the assumption by first dispersing with termination detection and electing a leader, after which a spanning tree lets the agents compute $\Delta$ and the largest identifier themselves [Chand2026Triangle]; knowing only that largest identifier $L$ is a weaker assumption, recorded on results rather than as a level of this axis [Chand2025Trees]. For maximal independent sets the introductory algorithms assume $n$ and $\Delta$ from dispersed and arbitrary starts and nothing from a rooted start (Theorems 3.1, 3.4 and 3.5 of [Pattanayak2024MIS]); [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE] and [Kaur2026MIS] remove the assumption for every start.

variants.title: Knowing $n$ and $\Delta$
variants.summary: With $n$ and $\Delta$ known: $O(n\log^2 n+D\Delta\log n)$ rounds from any start with $O(\log n)$ bits; from a rooted start $O(n\Delta)$ rounds need no knowledge.

results.note: Theorems 3.4 and 3.5: $O(n\Delta\log n)$ rounds from dispersed and arbitrary starts. From a rooted start $O(n\Delta)$ rounds with no knowledge (Theorem 3.1, listed under the rooted setting). Trees: $O(D^2)$ rounds from a rooted start with $O(\log n)$ bits (Theorem 4.2); $O(D)$ rounds from a dispersed start knowing $\Delta$, and $O(n)$ rounds from an arbitrary start knowing $n$ and $\Delta$, both with $O(\Delta+\log n)$ bits (Theorems 4.3 and 4.4). Rectangular grids of $x \times y$ nodes: $O(\max(x, y))$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits, knowing $x$ and $y$ (Theorem 5.1).
Theorem 3: elect a leader (Theorem 1), then build the set from the dispersed configuration.

variants.title: No knowledge
variants.summary: Without knowledge: $O(\max\{n\log^2 n, m\})$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits.

variants.title: Rooted start, no knowledge
variants.summary: From a rooted start without knowledge of $n$ or $\Delta$, an MIS takes $O(n\Delta)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3.1, Algorithm MIS-GraphRooted): a depth-first traversal that settles one agent on each new node, while the unsettled agents visit the neighbours of that node to learn whether one of them is already in the set; at most $4m$ rounds of traversal and $2\delta$ rounds of visits at a node of degree $\delta$. No knowledge of graph parameters. On trees, $O(D^2)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits (Theorem 4.2).

time.note: No lower bound. From an arbitrary start, $O(\max\{n\log^2 n, m\})$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits [Kaur2026MIS] carry over and are faster when $m = o(n\Delta)$ and $\Delta$ exceeds $\log^2 n$.

memory.note: [Pattanayak2024MIS] call $O(\log n)$ bits optimal because an agent stores its ID; no lower bound is recorded here.

variants.notes: The rooted start is all $n$ agents on one node (initial axis of the model). From the same start, [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE] need $O(n\Delta)$ rounds and $O(n\log n)$ bits (Theorem 20), which this result dominates. Checked against the full text of [Pattanayak2024MIS].

figure.caption: MIS by a depth-first walk that colours as it settles [Chand2023Cover] (other algorithms, e.g. from an arbitrary start, in [Pattanayak2024MIS]): all agents start at node $a$; the group moves one edge per round in depth-first order (the walk's tree is drawn in grey), and at each empty node the agent with the smallest ID settles. A settled agent whose parent is black turns grey at once; otherwise it visits each neighbour and comes back, and turns black only if none is black. The black nodes form a maximal independent set.
